taxonomy.subtopic: Reduced beta-globin synthesis and ineffective erythropoiesis

questions.stem_html:
A 19-year-old man of Mediterranean ancestry is evaluated for chronic fatigue. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL, MCV is 64 fL, ferritin is normal, and the erythrocyte count is relatively high for the hemoglobin level. The smear shows target cells and basophilic stippling. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbA2 and mildly increased HbF.

Which cellular abnormality is chiefly responsible for his anemia?

options.text_html: Oxidant-induced denaturation of hemoglobin into Heinz bodies
Autoantibody binding to red-cell membrane proteins at body temperature
Defective heme synthesis from iron depletion
Loss of the red-cell membrane skeleton through spectrin deficiency
Excess unpaired alpha-globin chains precipitate in erythroid precursors and cause ineffective erythropoiesis

questions.explanation_html: Reduced beta-chain production leaves alpha chains unpaired. Their precipitation damages marrow erythroblasts and circulating red cells, causing ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis. Microcytosis with normal iron stores, a relatively preserved red-cell count, target cells, and elevated HbA2 is classic for beta-thalassemia trait.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Heinz bodies are associated with oxidant injury such as G6PD deficiency or unstable hemoglobins.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Warm autoimmune hemolysis causes spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not marked microcytosis with elevated HbA2.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Iron deficiency lowers ferritin and usually does not increase HbA2.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis and increased osmotic fragility.

questions.educational_objective: Explain beta-thalassemia anemia through globin-chain imbalance, alpha-chain precipitation, ineffective erythropoiesis, and the characteristic electrophoresis pattern.
